description.summary: The alleged psychic or miraculous ability to be — or to appear to be — physically present in two distinct places at the same time. Reported in Catholic hagiography, Hindu and Buddhist siddhi literature, and parapsychology.
description.full: Bilocation (also called multilocation) is the alleged ability of a person, or rarely an object, to be present in two distinct physical places simultaneously. The concept appears across many religious and esoteric traditions. In the Catholic Church, bilocation is recorded as a charism of the saints, with classic cases attributed to Saint Anthony of Padua, Saint Francis Xavier, Saint Martin de Porres, the Venerable María de Ágreda, and — most famously in the 20th century — Saint Padre Pio of Pietrelcina. In Hindu and Buddhist traditions, bilocation is one of the siddhis, ascribed in the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. Parallel concepts appear in Theosophy, Sufism, Jewish mysticism, and shamanism. Catholic theologians distinguish between substantial bilocation (the saint physically present in two places) and apparitional bilocation (a non-substantial visible double appearing while the saint remains in one place). Skeptics, including Joe Nickell and the parapsychology critic Susan Blackmore, note that no case of bilocation has been verified under controlled conditions and that all evidence is anecdotal.

etymology.meaning: 'Two-placed' — the state of being in two places at once.
etymology.first_use: Latin theological usage from the late medieval / early modern period; English from at least the 19th century.

related_phenomena.name: Doppelgänger
related_phenomena.description: Germanic 'double-walker' — apparition of a living person, often as an omen

related_phenomena.name: Out-of-body experience
related_phenomena.description: Subjective sense of separation from the body

related_phenomena.name: Remote viewing
related_phenomena.description: Claimed psychic perception of distant locations

related_phenomena.name: Crisis apparition
related_phenomena.description: Reported appearance of a person at the moment of their death or distress

related_phenomena.name: Psychic phenomena (siddhis)
related_phenomena.description: Yogic and parapsychological category to which bilocation belongs

features.description: The defining feature: a witness reports the subject in one location while other witnesses see them, contemporaneously, somewhere else.
The two appearances may be on different continents (e.g. Padre Pio cases) and at distances that make conventional travel impossible in the time available.

features.feature: Sometimes accompanied by trance or ecstasy
features.description: The subject in their 'home' location is often reported in deep prayer or trance during the bilocation.

features.feature: Verbal exchanges with the second presence
features.description: Hagiographies often record meaningful conversations between the saint's distant double and witnesses.

physical.morphology: The 'second presence' is variably described as fully solid (substantial bilocation) or as a luminous or translucent figure (apparitional bilocation).

abilities.description: The subject is reported as physically present in both places; objects can be touched and exchanged.
The subject's double appears as an apparition while the body remains in one place.
Some accounts (María de Ágreda) extend bilocation to claimed missionary visits across oceans.

habitat_preference: Times of crisis or imminent death
patterns: Often associated with deep prayer, trance, or mystical ecstasy
Frequently reported around the time of crises affecting the witnesses
Many cases involve the figure delivering a message or aid

range.description: Globally distributed in religious and folkloric tradition: Catholic Europe and Latin America (Marian apparitions, saintly bilocations), Hindu and Buddhist Asia (yogic siddhis), Norse and Finnish Europe (vardøger, etiäinen), and modern parapsychology.

first_recorded.source: Pythagorean tradition (Pythagoras reportedly seen in Metapontum and Tauromenium simultaneously)

peak_activity_periods.description: Era of the most extensively documented Catholic bilocation cases (Anthony of Padua, María de Ágreda, Joseph of Cupertino)
Padre Pio bilocation reports and parapsychological investigations

origins.cultural_roots: Pythagorean / classical Greek hagiography, Catholic mystical theology, Hindu yogic siddhi tradition, and Northern European folkloric doubles (vardøger, etiäinen, doppelgänger).
origins.earliest_accounts: Classical reports of Pythagoras seen in two cities at once; later Apollonius of Tyana traditions.
origins.folklore_connections: Closely connected to doppelgänger and crisis-apparition lore in Europe; to siddhi traditions in South Asia.

timeline.event: Pythagoras reportedly seen at Metapontum (Italy) and Tauromenium (Sicily) on the same day
timeline.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers (3rd century CE)

timeline.event: Saint Anthony of Padua reportedly bilocates between Limoges (France) and Lisbon (Portugal) during Holy Thursday
Spanish nun María de Ágreda reportedly bilocates from her convent in Spain to evangelise the Jumano people of New Mexico
timeline.significance: Famous early modern case, with Spanish missionary cross-references

timeline.event: Saint Alphonsus Liguori reportedly bilocates from Arezzo to be at the deathbed of Pope Clement XIV in Rome
Padre Pio reportedly bilocates to Uruguay to attend Archbishop Antonio María Barbieri
timeline.source: Pasquale di Cicco testimony; Catholic biographies of Padre Pio

timeline.event: Death of Padre Pio at San Giovanni Rotondo; canonised by Pope John Paul II in 2002
timeline.significance: Modern Catholic figure most associated with bilocation

history.modern_era: Bilocation remains a feature of Catholic hagiography and folk Catholic devotion (especially around Padre Pio shrines), and a fringe topic in parapsychology. Mainstream science treats the claim as unverified and most likely an artefact of misidentification, deliberate mystification, or coincidence.

notable.name: Saint Anthony of Padua at Limoges and Lisbon

types: Members of two Franciscan communities (per hagiography)
credibility_factors: Multiple-witness tradition reported in later Franciscan sources

notable.description: While preaching at Holy Thursday liturgy in Limoges, Anthony reportedly recalled a missed monastic obligation in another church across town (some traditions say in Lisbon), knelt, became motionless, and was simultaneously seen at the second site reading the appointed lesson before disappearing.

notable.name: Sor María de Jesús de Ágreda — Jumano missionary bilocations

location.description: Convent of the Conceptionists, Ágreda, Spain — to the Jumano people in present-day New Mexico/Texas

credibility_factors: Franciscan corroboration via the 1630 Benavides Memorial

notable.description: Sor María, a Spanish Conceptionist nun who never left her cloister, reportedly experienced more than 500 mystical bilocations to evangelise the Jumano people of New Mexico between 1620 and 1623. Franciscan friars in the region, led by Alonso de Benavides, reported encountering Indigenous people who claimed to have been instructed by 'the Lady in Blue', whose description matched Sor María.

factors: Sor María herself later expressed uncertainty
credibility.notes: One of the most cited and most studied bilocation cases.

notable.name: Alphonsus Liguori at the deathbed of Pope Clement XIV

types: Liguori himself, attendants, and (per hagiography) papal household
credibility_factors: Multiple ecclesiastical witnesses cited in canonisation record

notable.description: Saint Alphonsus Liguori reportedly fell into a long trance while preparing for Mass at Arezzo and, on awaking, said that he had been at the deathbed of Pope Clement XIV in Rome (about 200 km away). Witnesses at the papal court reportedly identified Liguori among those present.
sources: Tannoia, A. (1798), Vita di Sant'Alfonso Maria de'Liguori

notable.name: Padre Pio in San Giovanni Rotondo and Montevideo

types: Friars at San Giovanni Rotondo (per Capuchin testimony)

notable.description: Padre Pio is reported to have appeared at the bedside of the future Cardinal Antonio María Barbieri's friend in Uruguay while remaining at the Capuchin friary in San Giovanni Rotondo. Barbieri later identified Pio when he visited Italy.

documentary.name: Benavides Memorial (1630)
documentary.description: Spanish Franciscan Alonso de Benavides's report to King Philip IV and the Holy See documenting Indigenous accounts of 'the Lady in Blue' in New Mexico, identified with Sor María de Ágreda.
documentary.analysis: Foundational document for the María de Ágreda bilocation case; viewed by historians as evidence of cross-cultural communication and missionary self-fashioning rather than as proof of bilocation.

documentary.name: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali — siddhi pāda
documentary.description: Sanskrit text describing siddhis attainable through yogic practice, including powers conventionally interpreted as bilocation.
documentary.analysis: Locus classicus for the South Asian formulation of bilocation as a yogic ability.

paranormal.name: Charism of the saints (Catholic)
paranormal.description: Bilocation is a divinely granted gift (charism) by which God permits a saint to appear simultaneously in two places, either substantially or apparitionally.
evidence_cited: Canonisation processes (Anthony of Padua, Liguori, Padre Pio)

paranormal.name: Yogic siddhi
paranormal.description: Bilocation is one of the powers attainable by an advanced practitioner of yoga, listed among the siddhis in Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.

paranormal.name: Astral projection / etheric double
paranormal.description: Theosophical and modern occult traditions explain bilocation as projection of an etheric double (or astral body) while the physical body remains in place.

scientific.name: Misidentification and coincidence
scientific.description: Many cases reduce on examination to mistaken identity by witnesses, telescoped chronology in retelling, or coincidence between independent events.
evidence_cited: Joe Nickell's investigations of Padre Pio cases

scientific.name: Hagiographic accretion
scientific.description: Long after a saint's death, additional bilocation episodes accrete to the biography, expressing the community's theology of the saint's continuing presence.
evidence_cited: Comparative analysis of medieval miracle collections

skeptical.name: No controlled evidence
skeptical.description: Despite a century of parapsychological interest, no case of bilocation has been replicated or evidenced under controlled conditions; all evidence is anecdotal.
evidence_cited: Skeptical reviews of Padre Pio testimony

traditions: Catholic hagiography (Anthony of Padua, María de Ágreda, Liguori, Padre Pio)
stories: The Lady in Blue (Sor María de Ágreda) and the Jumano
folklore.beliefs: Bilocation continues to be cited in popular Catholic devotion, particularly around the Padre Pio cult; it is treated metaphorically in modern psychic and New Age literature.

literature: Mystical City of God — María de Ágreda (1670)
Padre Pio: The True Story — C. Bernard Ruffin (1991)
Lives of the Saints (multiple editions, e.g. Butler)
film_tv: Numerous Catholic documentaries on saintly miracles
other: 'Bilocation' as a frequent metaphor in literature and modern psychic-themed fiction

researchers.name: Joe Nickell
researchers.contribution: Skeptical investigation of Catholic miracle claims, including bilocation

researchers.name: Susan Blackmore
researchers.contribution: Skeptical analysis of out-of-body and related anomalous experiences

research.ongoing_studies: No active mainstream scientific research; bilocation remains a topic of theological reflection in Catholicism and a sometimes-cited topic in fringe parapsychology.
